entities.summary:
Košice, the largest city in eastern Slovakia, has served as a vital hub throughout the medieval period, particularly from its founding in the 13th century. Established in 1230, it emerged as a significant trade center due to its strategic location along the important trade routes connecting the Kingdom of Hungary with Poland and other regions of Europe. Its prosperity attracted craftsmen and merchants, fostering a diverse urban culture that would influence the region's development in subsequent centuries.

By the late 14th century, Košice had gained considerable autonomy, earning the title of a free royal town in 1369, which allowed it to govern its own affairs and establish a self-sustaining economy. The city became known for its rich Gothic architecture, exemplified by the magnificent St. Elisabeth Cathedral, which was completed in the early 15th century. Košice also played a key role in the regional politics of the time, notably when it hosted the assembly of the nobles in 1471 that determined the future of the Hungarian crown during a contentious succession crisis.

The legacy of Košice extends beyond its medieval prominence, influencing the national identity of Slovakia as it became a symbol of urban development and civic autonomy. The city's historical role as a center of commerce and culture paved the way for its recognition as an important cultural capital in the modern era, contributing to Slovakia's national consciousness especially during the 20th century. Today, Košice stands as the second-largest city in Slovakia, reflective of its enduring significance in the region's history.

Košice is not only a historical testament to medieval urban life but also a living archive of the influences of various cultures, including Hungarian, German, and Slovak. As historian János Károlyi remarked, 'The pulse of medieval Europe can still be felt in the cobblestone streets of Košice.'
